nutshell: Object-level spatial AI systems (robotics/SLAM/AR) need to be taught new objects at run-time from a single or few examples, but few-shot segmentation, video object segmentation (VOS), and re-identification have historically been studied in isolation and none jointly solve single/few-shot instance segmentation plus re-identification across changing scene contexts. ISAR is a new semi-synthetic benchmark (Habitat simulator, Replica/HM3D indoor scenes, YCB objects) unifying these three tasks, along with a training-free baseline method (SAM segmentation + DINOv2 pixel features + per-object linear SVM) for reference. This paper is not person-ReID - it's a general object-level segmentation/re-ID benchmark pulled in by broader search terms.
contributions: ISAR benchmark: 24 test cases (each with single-shot and multi-shot annotation variants) totaling 84 semi-synthetic RGB(-D) video sequences with pixel-perfect ground-truth masks (via Habitat simulator rendering of Replica/HM3D scenes with YCB objects), explicitly designed to require generalizing object identity across distinct scene contexts rather than simple within-scene mask propagation like standard VOS benchmarks.

A new evaluation protocol tailored to the joint task: separate metrics for when an object is visible (Jaccard index, boundary F1-score, visible misclassification/false-detection rates) versus not visible (non-visible false-detection rate) - existing VOS metrics don't distinguish these cases.
Per-sequence attribute tagging (dynamic objects, clutter, same-class distractors, small objects, fast camera motion) inspired by DAVIS, enabling fine-grained failure-mode analysis by scenario type.

A zero-training baseline: SAM converts a point/bbox annotation into an initial mask, DINOv2 dense features trained via a per-object linear SVM (with negatives both outside the mask and from a diverse background pool) classify pixels in new frames, with an optional SAM-based mask-refinement step - the method needs no task-specific training and is class-agnostic.
deficiencies: As a brand-new benchmark, the paper's Table 3 results are the baseline's absolute numbers with no other published method run for comparison - it can't yet demonstrate that the benchmark actually discriminates good methods from bad ones beyond the paper's own internal ablations (feature choice, refinement step).

Absolute baseline performance is very low: mean Jaccard is only 0.269 (single-shot) / 0.322 (multi-shot), and the visible misclassification rate (fraction of visible-object frames with J < 0.4) is 0.71 / 0.65 - meaning the released baseline gets barely any correct overlap on the majority of frames where the object is actually visible, leaving little signal about what 'good' looks like on this benchmark yet.

The baseline processes each frame independently with no temporal propagation, despite the benchmark being built from video and despite the paper's own related-work section arguing this is exactly VOS's advantage - the paper's own qualitative analysis (Sec 6.3) attributes frame-to-frame mask instability directly to this omission, so the reference baseline doesn't showcase the video-centric angle the benchmark is motivated by.

The dataset is semi-synthetic (simulator renders with composited YCB objects) - realism and domain gap to real sensor noise, motion blur, and real-world occlusion patterns are never discussed or validated against any real-data subset.
notable: The feature-backbone ablation (Sec 6.5, Fig. 5) found DINOv2 dense features clearly beat both SAM's own internal features and CLIP for distinguishing two visually similar instances of the same class (e.g. a flat vs. crosshead screwdriver) - useful for anyone picking an off-the-shelf backbone for instance-level (not just class-level) description. The SAM mask-refinement step is a nice double-edged finding: it improves boundary F1 and same-class disambiguation but actively hurts multi-part objects, since SAM tends to propose one mask per part rather than one mask for the whole object (Fig. 6).
